question.text: India deposited its instrument of ratification of the Multilateral Instrument (MLI) with OECD on 25 June 2019 (in force from 1 October 2019). From a Cat II AIF manager's perspective advising non-resident LPs, what is the MOST important substantive change the MLI brings to India's treaty network?

answer.text: Automatic withdrawal of all treaty benefits for non-residents
A new TDS rate of 20% on every outbound payment
Mandatory 5% India-resident investor participation limit in every AIF
Modification of India's tax-treaty network to prevent Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) and the inappropriate granting of treaty benefits, including treaty-shopping arrangements

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook describes the MLI as modifying India's tax-treaty network to prevent BEPS and the inappropriate granting of treaty benefits, including treaty-shopping arrangements. India's MLI positions and the modifications to specific covered treaties are given effect through the existing Section 90(1) framework of the ITA. This treaty-modification function is the substantive change a Cat II AIF manager advising non-resident LPs must monitor when relying on a treaty benefit. The Trap: Option A overstates the MLI — it modifies treaties, it does not cancel them wholesale. Option B invents a TDS rate. Option C confuses MLI with the Section 9A onshore-management conditions. Note: The workbook frames the MLI under BEPS Action Plan 15 (the multilateral instrument itself) and ties India's adoption to Section 90(1). Specific anti-abuse tests applied through a particular treaty should be checked against that treaty's text and India's MLI notifications.
